title: NumPy
description: Learn numerical computing with NumPy arrays and perform efficient mathematical operations on data.
objectives: Create NumPy arrays and inspect shape, dtype, and size.
Select data with indexing, slicing, and boolean masks.
Reshape arrays without copying the underlying data.
Use broadcasting and vectorised math instead of Python loops.

slides.title: NumPy
slides.lead: NumPy is the numerical engine underneath Pandas, Matplotlib, and every machine learning library in Python.
bullets: One data type per array, stored in one contiguous block of memory
Operations apply to the whole array at once  no loops
10–100× faster than equivalent Python list code
Import convention: import numpy as np

slides.title: Creating arrays
slides.lead: An ndarray is a grid of values, all of the same type, with a shape describing its dimensions.
bullets: np.array([...]) from an existing list
np.zeros(n), np.ones(n), np.full(n, value)
np.arange(start, stop, step)  like range, but an array
np.linspace(start, stop, count)  evenly spaced, stop included
np.random.rand(n) / np.random.randint(low, high, n)

slides.title: Array vs list  the real difference
slides.lead: The same expression means two different things depending on the type.
bullets: [1, 2] * 2 gives [1, 2, 1, 2]  the list repeats
np.array([1, 2]) * 2 gives [2, 4]  every element is multiplied
Arrays have one dtype; a list can mix types
Arrays are fixed size; append means building a new array
Arrays support math operators element-wise
slides.note: argmax returns the position of the largest value, not the value  useful for looking up the matching name in another array.

slides.title: Indexing, including boolean masks
slides.lead: Comparing an array to a value gives an array of True/False, which you can use to select rows.

body: print(mask)                         # [ True True True False True]
# combine conditions with & and |, wrap each in ()

slides.note: Use & and |  not the keywords and / or. Python's keywords cannot work element-wise and will raise a ValueError.

slides.title: Slicing returns a view, not a copy
slides.lead: This is NumPy's biggest surprise: writing into a slice changes the original array.

body: safe = a[1:4].copy()   # take a copy when you need independence

slides.title: Broadcasting  arrays of different shapes
slides.lead: NumPy stretches the smaller array across the larger one when their shapes are compatible, without copying memory.
bullets: Shapes are compared from the right
Dimensions match if they are equal, or if one of them is 1
A single number broadcasts to any shape
A row of shape (3,) broadcasts across every row of a (2, 3) array
Incompatible shapes raise ValueError: operands could not be broadcast

body: print(grid * weights)             # applied to each row
print(grid + col)                 # applied to each column

slides.title: Vectorised math and aggregations
slides.lead: Aggregations collapse an array to a summary. On 2D arrays, axis picks the direction.
slides.note: axis=0 means "collapse the rows", giving one result per column. axis=1 is the opposite. Say it out loud until it sticks.

slides.title: Practice: exam analysis without loops
slides.lead: Given a (5, 3) array of scores  5 students, 3 subjects  produce each result with a single NumPy expression.
bullets: Each student's average across the 3 subjects
Each subject's highest score
A boolean mask of students whose average is at least 75
The scores array with every failing score (< 50) replaced by 50
The whole array rescaled so each subject runs 0 to 1
slides.note: Build the data with np.random.randint(35, 100, (5, 3)) and set np.random.seed(0) first so your numbers are reproducible.

slides.title: Module 03 recap
slides.lead: You can now express calculations over whole datasets without writing a loop.
bullets: shape, dtype, and ndim describe every array
Boolean masks are how you filter numerical data
Slices are views  copy when you need independence
Broadcasting removes the need to reshape by hand
axis=0 collapses rows, axis=1 collapses columns
